Cordell Hull
Hudson Mitchell-Pullman
The Franklin Delano Roosevelt (FDR) Administration
The Great Depression 1933-1937
Section 1: Historical Background
We are in the midst of a global social and economic catastrophe, and this cabinet must
work urgently to revitalize our economy and address issues that stretch beyond our borders. The
Wall Street Crash of 1929, our inability to control monetary policy due to our use of the Gold
Standard, and the Federal Reserve’s indecisiveness and absence of action have all contributed to
the dire economic situation in which the United States currently finds itself. From 1929 to the
present, the United States Real GDP has fallen by nearly 30 percent, and unemployment has
peaked at 25 percent. More than 9,000 banks have failed nationwide, and depositors have lost
over 1.3 billion dollars. However, reverting to isolationism and a global lack of coordination and
cooperation have greatly exacerbated the Great Depression. A plethora of countries, including
the United States and France, continue to follow strict adherence to the Gold Standard, even after
the United Kingdom abandoned it in 1931. This has led to a rise in global protectionism, causing
harmful trade legislation, which includes the ineffective Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act. Although
these tariffs aim to protect America’s struggling farmers, who make up roughly 20 percent of the
US population, they result in tax increases on over 900 different imported goods by an average of
40 to 60 percent, placing an economic burden on American consumers. These tariffs have raised
the prices of consumer goods, caused the stock market to crash further following the 1929 crash,
and most devastatingly, encourage retaliatory action by other nations, including America’s
biggest trading partner, Canada. This has caused US exports to plummet and global trade to fall
by 65 percent, making it nearly insurmountable for the US and other countries to overcome the
global economic depression. This inward-focused approach has also caused a dangerous rise in
both fascism and expansionism across Europe and Asia, threatening the US economy and
national security. Adolf Hitler, the Nazi Party’s extremist leader, was recently elected chancellor
of Germany. Additionally, Benito Mussolini, a dangerous fascist dictator, currently controls Italy,
and Japan, fueled by expansionist desires, invaded Manchuria, China, two years ago in 1931.
Section 2: Cordell Hull’s Position
As the United States Secretary of State, I hope to use trade liberalization to improve the
US’s economic, political, and societal standing both domestically and globally. Mounting
pressure from Americans to improve our dire economic situation domestically has caused an
understandable halt in support of free trade initiatives; however, I believe that free trade is a vital
aspect of improving the domestic and global economy. Additionally, although isolationist
rhetoric by the US and other European nations has caused indifference regarding trade
liberalization on a multilateral level, I find it to be impossible to separate the idea of global
commerce from world peace. Dating back to our founding father Benjamin Franklin, we have
traditionally had a policy of free and open trade with equal access to all markets, however, we
have resorted to “beggar-thy-neighbor” trade policies as a result of these extreme economic
difficulties. Our closed markets, preferential and exclusive trade agreements, and import tariffs
only benefit an insignificant number of special interest groups. Instead, they have caused
Americans economic troubles and have caused political friction and fragility. The biggest
challenge that we face as fellow members of FDR’s brain trust is demonstrating to the American
people, and skeptics in Congress, that unhampered global trade is the only viable method of
fostering world economic prosperity and peace.
Section 3: Solutions
Before we begin drafting potential legislative action and executive orders, we must first
convince the American people that focusing on trade liberalization and global collaboration will
Cordell Hull
Hudson Mitchell-Pullman
The Franklin Delano Roosevelt (FDR) Administration
The Great Depression 1933-1937
benefit economic interests both in America and abroad, in addition to maintaining world order.
First, I plan to immediately centralize American trade policy by establishing a branch of the State
Department that solely focuses on international trade policies and negotiations. This bureau will
begin by creating targeted marketing campaigns through newspapers, TV and radio ads, and
press conferences to target everyday Americans and members of Congress. The objective of
these outreach efforts is to garner excitement and public support for liberalized trade. To
reinvigorate support for trade liberalization on a multilateral level, the specialized trade bureau
will host global trade summits and forums to discuss the immense benefits of a coordinated
global trade liberalization effort. Furthermore, the US must negotiate with France and other
nations still using the Gold Standard to allow for an immediate and seamless transition from the
Gold Standard to a fluctuating currency. I propose that we allow these countries to temporarily
peg their currency to the USD at a fixed rate with a small range of acceptable variation to prevent
devaluation wars, should they agree to leave the Gold Standard. Additionally, the US will reduce
or eliminate tariffs on nations who agree to leave the Gold Standard and implement reciprocal
trade agreements, allowing for rapid economic recovery domestically while also liberalizing
trade globally. To kickstart global trade, the US should also increase imports of certain products
while ensuring that we protect our agricultural and manufacturing industries at home. We must
also use public works projects and infrastructure upgrades to increase domestic production of
goods that can be exported to other nations. This will further contribute to the national and
international economic recovery. Lastly, global economic instability is threatened by the rise of
extremist governments worldwide. I believe that world peace is only possible with global
economic prosperity. Therefore, we must use effective multilateral economic policy and
unprecedented levels of worldwide cooperation to combat rising expansionism. We should also
join and lead reforms in the League of Nations, impose sanctions on aggressor nations, namely
Japan, Germany, and Italy, and form strong military alliances with allied nations to defend
against potentially harmful nations. We must also contribute to the economic recovery of
lesser-developed nations, including those in Latin America, without interfering militarily. The
administration shall also increase military spending and the amount of private sector military
contracts to act as a deterrent to a potential world war by adversarial nations.
